title: SpreadCluster: Recovering Versioned Spreadsheets through Similarity-Based Clustering
research_question: Can spreadsheet versions whose explicit version history has been lost be recovered reliably by clustering spreadsheets according to structural and textual similarities in their worksheets and table headers?
methodology: The authors first inspect known spreadsheet evolution groups and identify table headers and worksheet names as useful version-related features. SpreadCluster extracts and cleans these features, computes worksheet similarity using textual representations of header contents together with worksheet-name information, derives spreadsheet-level similarities, and applies an adapted single-linkage clustering procedure. Similarity thresholds are learned by sweeping candidate threshold values against a manually curated training set derived from VEnron. The approach is then evaluated on Enron, EUSES, and FUSE spreadsheet corpora and compared with a filename-based version-recovery method.

key_findings.finding: On the Enron evaluation, SpreadCluster produced 1,561 candidate evolution groups, of which 1,226 were manually validated as correct, corresponding to 78.5% precision.
Against the constructed Enron ground truth of 1,609 evolution groups, SpreadCluster achieved 70.7% recall and a 74.4% F-measure.
The filename-based comparison method achieved 59.8% precision, 48.7% recall, and 53.7% F-measure on the same evaluation, substantially below the reported SpreadCluster metrics.
The learned worksheet- and spreadsheet-level similarity thresholds were 0.60 and 0.33 respectively after threshold search on the curated training data.
On EUSES the method reported 170 correct groups among 213 detected groups, or 79.8% precision, while a manually inspected sample of 200 FUSE groups produced 91.0% precision.

The recovered VEnron2 collection contains substantially more spreadsheet evolution groups and spreadsheets than the earlier VEnron collection, demonstrating that content-based recovery can expose additional version relationships missed by the earlier construction.

SpreadCluster clusters spreadsheets into evolution groups but does not automatically recover the chronological or parent-child ordering of versions; the paper states that version order was recovered manually and leaves automatic ordering for future work.

limitations: The method recovers membership in version/evolution groups rather than a directed lineage graph or automatic chronological ordering among individual spreadsheet versions.
Parallel evolution or branching versions are placed in the same evolution group rather than explicitly represented as forks in a provenance graph.
Header extraction is heuristic and can fail for spreadsheets containing primarily numerical or date-like headers, charts, data without recognizable headers, or other atypical layouts.
Worksheets with little meaningful content or generic worksheet names provide weak discriminative evidence.

The Enron ground truth was constructed using manual validation and the union of candidates found by SpreadCluster and a filename-based method, so evolution groups missed by both methods could remain absent.
Manual validation can introduce judgment errors despite cross-checking by multiple authors.
The authors identify representativeness of the evaluated spreadsheet corpora as a threat to external validity.
No public implementation of SpreadCluster was reported in the paper.
raw_claims: Spreadsheet files frequently lose explicit version information when they are copied, renamed, emailed, or moved.
Versions belonging to the same evolution group often retain similar worksheet names and table headers.
SpreadCluster uses worksheet names and table-header contents as its principal similarity features.
Formula text is not used as a principal version feature because ordinary spreadsheet evolution can change formulas even when versions remain closely related.
Spreadsheet similarity is derived from similarities among worksheets and then used by a clustering procedure.
Threshold parameters are learned from a manually curated set of known spreadsheet evolution groups.
SpreadCluster reports higher precision, recall, and F-measure than the filename-based comparison on the Enron evaluation.
The method was evaluated on spreadsheet collections from Enron, EUSES, and FUSE.
The resulting VEnron2 dataset expands the set of known evolution groups beyond the earlier VEnron dataset.
The reported method does not itself infer version ordering inside an evolution group.
Automatic recovery of version order is identified as future work.
